newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine judge questioned admiral on Dirty War.
newsitem.headline: Argentine judge questioned admiral on Dirty War.

text.p: An Argentine judge has said he interviewed one of the leaders of the 1976 military coup to seek details about the fate of thousands of people who disappeared during the military's six-year reign of terror.

Federal Judge Eduardo Luraschi told Clarin newspaper in a report published on Wednesday that he met former Adm. Eduardo Massera but denied a deal had been cut for Massera to reveal secret files on those who disappeared in the "Dirty War" against suspected leftists in exchange for being left alone.
"Yes, I met with Massera," said the judge. "But there are no negotiations of any sort. I have nothing to negotiate. What we are trying to find out is the fate of the missing people."
It is officially estimated that 10,000 people disappeared in the Dirty War though human rights groups put the number of victims nearer to 30,000.

Relatives of the victims, led by the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, insist that the military must have secret information about what happened to their loved ones and where they were buried, but the military has repeatedly denied this.
Massera and other Dirty War officers were tried for their crimes after democracy was restored in 1983, but walked free after President Carlos Menem declared an amnesty in 1989.

Now Spanish and Italian judges want these officers to give evidence about their citizens killed in the Dirty War and relatives of some prominent victims, such as Argentine writer Rodolfo Walsh who died in 1977, want to know where their remains are.

Clarin reported Monday Massera was offering information on the "desaparecidos" in exchange for being left alone, but the former admiral told local radio the same day: "I completely deny what Clarin says about me offering that information, simply because I don't have that information."
